title: Chapter 13: Bringing the Projects Together
content:
Chapter 13: Bringing the Projects Together

What the projects teach together

The first project introduced a single model call. The later projects placed that call inside applications that retrieve documents, run tools, store context and coordinate several steps. If you worked through them, you have seen how much of an AI application depends on ordinary software design: choosing inputs, handling errors, keeping state and checking the result.

The APIs and libraries will change. The questions behind the examples remain useful: What information does this task need? Which actions may the application take? How will you know when an answer is wrong? Keeping those questions in view makes it easier to adapt a project when its dependencies change.

What You Built

The projects below form a progression. Return to an earlier one whenever a later feature becomes difficult to explain or test.

ChapterProject
Chapter 1Python Code Explainer Assistant
Chapter 2Reusable Python LLM Client
Chapter 3Command-Line AI Assistant
Chapter 4Personal Document AI Assistant
Chapter 5Personal Knowledge Search Engine
Chapter 6API Tool-Using Agent
Chapter 7Personal Study or Work Assistant with Memory
Chapter 8Freelance Business Automation Agent
Chapter 9Research and Summary Agent
Chapter 10Guarded AI Assistant
Chapter 11AI Agent Evaluation Script
Chapter 12Personal AI Work Assistant

Each project can support a repository, a short demonstration, a blog post or a case study. Depending on the problem it addresses, it may also become a client demonstration, a service prototype or an early product experiment. Describe what you implemented and tested; a completed exercise by itself does not establish that a service is ready for customers.

The Personal AI Work Assistant from Chapter 12 is a useful project to develop further because it brings several parts together. Alternatively, choose the smaller project that most closely matches a problem you can observe and evaluate.

A design pattern you can reuse

Begin with the user’s goal, validate the input, and decide how the application will handle the request. Supply the model with the context it needs, use retrieval, tools or memory where the task calls for them, and check the result before presenting it or taking an action. Include human review wherever an incorrect decision would matter.

  1. Define the goal and acceptable result.
  2. Validate the input and select the workflow.
  3. Build the prompt and supply relevant context.
  4. Call the model and any permitted retrieval, memory or tool functions.
  5. Apply guardrails and validate the output.
  6. Obtain human review where required, then return the result.

You can adapt this pattern to document and study assistants, research workflows, proposal drafting, customer support, internal knowledge search and productivity dashboards. The components should follow the task: adding every feature from the book can make an otherwise simple application harder to understand.

Choosing the next improvement

Engineering judgement lies in deciding what belongs around a model call. A prompt needs an input contract; a tool needs validation and permissions; stored context needs a reason to be retained. Tests and evaluation give you evidence for deciding whether a change helped.

Start with the smallest version that serves your intended user. Add structure, retrieval, tools or memory as needed, then strengthen guardrails, evaluation, deployment and documentation. Keep a record of failures and use it to choose the next change. A feature is easier to maintain when you can explain the problem it solves.

Bonus Resources

Use these checklists and templates while building. They collect the decisions from the projects in a form you can revisit during development and review.

1. Python AI Agent Builder Checklist

Before you start, settle the scope and the evidence you will use to judge the result.

  • Define the user problem clearly.
  • Identify the target user.
  • Decide whether the app needs an LLM.
  • Decide whether the app needs RAG.
  • Decide whether the app needs tools.
  • Decide whether the app needs memory.
  • Decide whether human review is required.
  • Choose the AI provider or model.
  • Create a virtual environment.
  • Store API keys in environment variables or platform secrets.
  • Create a reusable LLM client.
  • Write clear system instructions.
  • Add prompt templates.
  • Validate user input.
  • Add error handling.
  • Add guardrails.
  • Add tests for normal Python logic.
  • Add evaluation cases for AI output.
  • Track cost and latency.
  • Document limitations.
  • Prepare deployment files.
  • Write a clear README.

2. RAG Debugging Checklist

When a document answer is weak, inspect extraction and retrieval before changing the answer prompt. These checks help you locate the failure.

  • Did the PDF text extract correctly?
  • Is the document digital text, not only scanned images?
  • Are chunks too small?
  • Are chunks too large?
  • Is overlap reasonable?
  • Is metadata stored?
  • Are source file names stored?
  • Are page numbers stored?
  • Are the retrieved chunks actually relevant?
  • Did you inspect retrieved chunks manually?
  • Does the prompt say to use only retrieved context?
  • Does the assistant say “not found” when appropriate?
  • Are source references shown?
  • Did you test unanswerable questions?
  • Did you test vague questions?
  • Did you test similar but different questions?

3. Prompt Templates for AI Agents

The following are literal starting prompts. Adapt them to your application’s inputs and output format, then evaluate their behaviour. Instructions in a prompt do not replace application-level permissions or validation.

General Assistant Prompt

You are a helpful AI assistant.

Rules:
- Be clear and practical.
- Do not invent facts.
- If information is missing, say what is missing.
- If the task is risky, recommend human review.
- Keep the answer appropriate for the user's skill level.

Python Tutor Prompt

You are a friendly Python tutor for beginner-to-intermediate learners.

Explain clearly.
Use simple examples.
Avoid unnecessary jargon.
Do not claim you executed code unless you actually did.
If code may contain a bug, explain it carefully.

RAG Answering Prompt

You are a careful document question-answering assistant.

Use only the provided document context.

If the answer is not in the context, say:
"I could not find that in the document."

Do not invent facts.
Do not use outside knowledge unless explicitly allowed.
When possible, mention the source page or section.

Tool-Using Agent Prompt

You are a tool-using AI assistant.

You may use only approved tools.
Do not invent tools.
Do not claim a tool was used unless it was actually called.
If a tool returns an error, explain the error clearly.
For risky actions, ask for human approval.

Workflow Automation Prompt

You are a practical workflow automation assistant.

Turn messy input into structured output.
Do not invent budget, deadline, or commitments.
Ask clarifying questions when details are missing.
Generate drafts for human review.
Do not claim anything was sent or submitted.

Reviewer Agent Prompt

You are a strict but helpful reviewer.

Check the draft for:
- Unsupported claims
- Missing context
- Confusing structure
- Overpromising
- Risky wording
- Missing human review notes

Return specific improvements.

4. Tool-Calling Function Template

Use this allowlisted registry when adding tools to an agent. The companion’s tool_template.py also includes a runnable demonstration and tests.

"""A small allowlisted tool registry from the book's bonus resources."""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable

ToolFunction = Callable[[str], str]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Tool:
    name: str
    description: str
    function: ToolFunction


def example_tool(tool_input: str) -> str:
    if not isinstance(tool_input, str) or not tool_input.strip():
        return "Tool error: input cannot be empty."
    return f"Processed: {tool_input}"


TOOLS = {
    "example_tool": Tool(
        name="example_tool",
        description="Use this tool for simple demonstration tasks.",
        function=example_tool,
    )
}


def is_allowed_tool(tool_name: str) -> bool:
    return isinstance(tool_name, str) and tool_name in TOOLS


def run_tool(tool_name: str, tool_input: str) -> str:
    if not is_allowed_tool(tool_name):
        return f"Tool error: {tool_name} is not allowed."
    return TOOLS[tool_name].function(tool_input)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(run_tool("example_tool", "Hello from Python"))

5. Guardrails Checklist

Review these behaviours with ordinary, malformed and adversarial inputs. A checklist describes what to test; it does not establish that the controls work.

  • Empty input is handled.
  • Long input is handled.
  • Secrets are not accepted or stored.
  • Risky actions are detected.
  • External actions require approval.
  • Destructive actions are blocked.
  • Sensitive professional advice is flagged.
  • Tool names are validated.
  • Tool inputs are validated.
  • Memory is user-controlled.
  • Users can inspect memory.
  • Users can delete memory.
  • RAG answers are grounded in context.
  • Unanswerable questions are handled.
  • Output is validated.
  • Human review checklist is shown when needed.
  • Limitations are documented.

6. AI Agent Evaluation Checklist

Keep test cases and observed results together so that a prompt or code change can be compared with the previous version.

  • Create evaluation test cases.
  • Include easy cases.
  • Include normal cases.
  • Include vague cases.
  • Include risky cases.
  • Include unanswerable cases.
  • Check expected keywords.
  • Check prohibited phrases.
  • Check required sections.
  • Track latency.
  • Estimate cost.
  • Log failures.
  • Review failed outputs manually.
  • Turn bugs into new test cases.
  • Save evaluation reports.
  • Retest after prompt changes.

7. Freelance AI Automation Service Ideas

8. Portfolio Project README Template

A reader should be able to understand the project, install it and identify its limits from the README. Use the outline below, replacing the illustrative names and commands where your project differs.

Project name and overview

Name the project, describe the user problem and explain what the application does. List its implemented features and its stack, such as Python, an LLM API, Streamlit or a CLI, Chroma or another store, and pytest.

Setup

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

Environment variables

OPENAI_API_KEY=your_key_here
OPENAI_MODEL=model_name

Run

python app.py

For a Streamlit application:

streamlit run app.py

Tests

python -m pytest

Screenshots, limits and future work

Add screenshots from your application, describe its limitations and list the improvements you intend to make. Include safety notes covering guardrails, review requirements and privacy. Keep planned features separate from implemented ones.

9. LLM Cost-Control Checklist

  • Use smaller models for simple tasks.
  • Avoid sending unnecessary context.
  • Retrieve only relevant chunks.
  • Limit output length.
  • Cache repeated results.
  • Avoid unnecessary multi-agent loops.
  • Test non-API logic without model calls.
  • Track number of model calls.
  • Estimate token usage.
  • Monitor provider billing dashboard.
  • Use normal Python when AI is not needed.
  • Summarize long memory instead of sending everything.
  • Avoid reprocessing the same PDF every time.

10. Suggested Learning Roadmap After This Book

Step 1: Strengthen Python Foundations

Review functions, classes, exceptions and file handling until you can explain them in your own projects. Practise virtual environments, testing, API calls, JSON and logging alongside that work.

Step 2: Improve AI App Architecture

Separate configuration, prompt templates and model calls from the application workflow. Study modular design, error handling, retries, logging and evaluation by improving a project you already understand.

Step 3: Go Deeper into RAG

Compare chunking strategies, embedding models and vector stores using questions from your own documents. Then investigate metadata filtering, hybrid search, citations and retrieval evaluation.

Step 4: Build Safer Tool Agents

Work on tool schemas, input validation, approval gates and API integrations. Distinguish read-only operations from actions that change external state, and keep an audit trail of what ran.

Step 5: Improve Deployment Skills

Develop your understanding of Streamlit, FastAPI, Docker and cloud deployment. Include secrets management, monitoring, authentication and database storage as the application’s needs grow.

Step 6: Build Portfolio Projects

Choose from the Personal Document AI Assistant, API Tool-Using Agent, Freelance Business Automation Agent, Research and Summary Agent, or Personal AI Work Assistant. Refine its setup, tests and documentation before moving on to another project.

Chapter 14 provides a glossary and a sequence for presenting that work. Use it when you are ready to explain the application to someone who has not followed your development process.
